On a question by Roggenkamp about group algebras

Dylan Johnston and Dmitriy Rumynin Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Warwick, Coventry, CV4 7AL, UK
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We investigate whether the group algebra of a finite group over a localisation of the integers is semiperfect. The main result is a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion in the ordinary case. In the modular case, we propose a conjecture, which extends the criterion.

Key words and phrases: 
Krull-Schmidt, semiperfect ring, group algebra, idempotent, finite group
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
16S34, 16U40, 20C20, 20C15

Introduction

In the present article we would like to contemplate the following problem, posed by Roggenkamp:

Problem 1.

[10, Kourovka Pr. 4.55] Let GG be a finite group and ℤ(p){\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)} the localization at pp. Does the Krull–Schmidt theorem hold for projective ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G-modules?

The first point to clarify is what is meant by the Krull-Schmidt theorem here. Note that in the literature the names of Azumaya and Remak are often attached to it as well, while it is normally formulated for the category of finite length modules with two slightly different, yet equivalent for finite length modules statements, cf. [3, 5] vs. [1, 6]. We can interpret Problem 1 as three different questions about ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G:

Problem 2.

Is the category of finitely generated projective ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G-modules a Krull-Schmidt category?

Problem 3.

Can every projective ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G-module PP be written as a direct sum of indecomposable projective modules P=⊕i∈IPiP=\oplus_{i\in I}P_{i} in a unique, up to a permutation and isomorphisms way?

Problem 4.

Can every finitely generated projective ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G-module PP be written as a direct sum of indecomposable projective modules

(1) P=P1⊕…⊕PnP=P_{1}\oplus\ldots\oplus P_{n}

in a unique, up to a permutation and isomorphisms way?

These problems are interdependent:

Yes to Pr. 2⟹Yes to Pr. 3⟹Yes to Pr. 4\mbox{Yes to Pr. 2}\Longrightarrow\mbox{Yes to Pr. 3}\Longrightarrow\mbox{Yes to Pr. 4}

In the present paper we address only Problem 2. The short answer to it is no. The reader can benefit from reading the expository paper by Krause [11]. The following well-known fact contains the definitions of a semiperfect ring and a Krull-Schmidt category.

Proposition 5.

[11, Prop. 4.1], [2, Th. 2.1], [3, Ch. 7] Let RR be a ring, J=J⁡(R)J=J(R) its Jacobson radical. The following conditions are equivalent:

  • •

    RR is semiperfect.

  • •

    The category of finitely generated projective left RR-modules is a Krull-Schmidt category.

  • •

    Every finitely generated projective left RR-module PP admits a decomposition (1) where each PiP_{i} has a local endomorphism ring.

  • •

    The regular module RR{}_{R}R admits a decomposition (1) where each PiP_{i} has a local endomorphism ring.

  • •

    Every simple left RR-module admits a projective cover.

  • •

    Every finitely generated left RR-module admits a projective cover.

  • •

    The ring R/JR/J is semisimple artinian and every idempotent in R/JR/J can be lifted to RR.

Now we can explain the negative answer to Problem 2, following Woods [14]. Let G=C3G=C_{3}, the cyclic group of order 33, 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} – the finite field of size qq. Observe that

(2) ℚ​C3≅ℚ⊕ℚ⁡(13),𝔽p​C3≅{𝔽p⊕𝔽p⊕𝔽p, if ​p≡1mod3,𝔽p⊕𝔽p2, if ​p≡2mod3.\mathbb{Q}C_{3}\cong\mathbb{Q}\oplus\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{1}),\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}C_{3}\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb{F}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{F}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{F}_{p}\,,&\ \mbox{ if }p\equiv 1\mod 3,\\ \mathbb{F}_{p}\oplus\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}\,,&\ \mbox{ if }p\equiv 2\mod 3.\end{cases}

If p≡1mod3p\equiv 1\mod 3, 𝔽p​G\mathbb{F}_{p}G has 3 primitive idempotents: too many to be lifted, so that ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is not semiperfect. On the other hand, if p≡2mod3p\equiv 2\mod 3, both primitive idempotents can be lifted to ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G, making it semiperfect:

13​(e+x+x2),13​(2​e−x−x2), where ​G=⟨x⟩.\frac{1}{3}(e+x+x^{2}),\ \frac{1}{3}(2e-x-x^{2}),\ \mbox{ where }\ G=\langle x\rangle\,.

Yet we are not satisfied with this brief negative answer. Consequently we reinterpret the original question:

Problem 6.

Let GG be a finite group and ℤ(p){\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)} the localisation at a prime pp. Find necessary and sufficient conditions on pp and GG for the ring ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G to be semiperfect.

Let us summarize quickly what is already known about it

Proposition 7.

The following statements hold for a finite group GG.

  1. (1)

    If N⊴GN\unlhd G and ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect, then ℤ(p)​G/N{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}G/N is semiperfect [2, Lemma 2.2].

  2. (2)

    ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect if and only if all idempotents of 𝔽p​G\mathbb{F}_{p}G can be lifted to ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G [4, Prop. 8].

  3. (3)

    Suppose N⊴GN\unlhd G, H≤GH\leq G, H​N=GHN=G and NN is a pp-group. If ℤ(p)​H{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}H is semiperfect, then ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect [14, Prop. 4.2].

  4. (4)

    ℤ(p)​S3{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}S_{3} is semiperfect for every pp [14, Lemma 6.1].

  5. (5)

    ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect if and only ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is clean (follows from [8, Th. 1.1]).

Assume further that GG is an abelian group of exponent n=m​pan=mp^{a}, p∤mp\nmid m with a Sylow pp-subgroup PP.

  1. (6)

    ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect if and only if ℤ(p)​G/P{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}G/P is semiperfect [14, Lemma 5.1].

  2. (7)

    ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect if and only if ℤ(p)​Cn{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}C_{n} is semiperfect [14, Prop. 5.7].

  3. (8)

    ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect if and only if each monic factor of zm−1∈𝔽p​[z]z^{m}-1\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[z] can be lifted to ℤ(p)​[z]{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}[z] [14, Th. 5.8].

  4. (9)

    ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect if and only pp is a primitive root of 1 modulo dd for each d|md|m [8, Lemma 2.6].

Notice further that a complete satisfactory answer to Problem 6 is known for abelian GG [8, Th. 2.11 and Th. 3.5], yet we skip it here as it boils down to getting to the bottom of the arithmetic of the last statement of Proposition 7.

For general GG and pp, the ring ℤ(p)​G/J{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G/J is semisimple and artinian – it is even a finite dimensional algebra. So the real issue is lifting of idempotents. The idempotents can be lifted to ℤ(p)^​G\widehat{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G, where ℤ(p)^\widehat{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}} is the pp-adic integers. This is a classical well-known topic [3, 5]: ℤ(p)^​G\widehat{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is always semiperfect. Here, in this paper, we are trying to grapple with the non-complete local ring ℤ(p){\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}.

We can give a fully satisfactory answer to Problem 6 only in the “ordinary” case. The answer can be given in terms of the standard arithmetic information attached to the complex irreducible characters χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\Irr(G).

Theorem 8.

Suppose pp doesn’t divide |G||G|. Then the ring ℤ(p)​G\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G is semiperfect if and only if both of the following conditions hold:

  1. i)

    For each χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\Irr(G) its Schur index ι⁡(χ)\iota(\chi) is 11.

  2. ii)

    For each χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\Irr(G) the prime pp is inert in the field of character values ℚ⁡(χ)\mathbb{Q}(\chi)

The modular case, when p||G|p\mid|G|, is harder to pinpoint. Yet we propose a conjecture that yields a workable criterion in the modular case.

To state it, we recall some standard notation.

Let RR be a ring. Let 𝐆⁡(R)\mathbf{G}(R) and 𝐊⁡(R)\mathbf{K}(R) denote the Grothendieck rings over ℤ\mathbb{Z} of finitely generated RR-modules and of finitely generated projective RR-modules, respectively. Let 𝐆+​(R)\mathbf{G}^{+}(R) and 𝐊+​(R)\mathbf{K}^{+}(R) be the corresponding positive Grothendieck semigroups, i.e., ℕ\mathbb{N}-spans of modules inside the Grothendieck groups. Consider the natural maps

(3) 𝐆⁡(ℚ​G)→𝛼𝐆⁡(𝔽p​G)←𝛽𝐊⁡(𝔽p​G)\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{Q}G)\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)\xleftarrow{\beta}\mathbf{K}(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)

where α\alpha is the decomposition map [5, Def. 16.20] and β\beta is the Cartan homomorphism [5, Def. 18.4].

Conjecture 9.

The ring ℤ(p)​G\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G is semiperfect if and only if α⁡(𝐆+​(ℚ​G))⊇β⁡(𝐊+​(𝔽p​G))\alpha(\mathbf{G}^{+}(\mathbb{Q}G))\supseteq\beta(\mathbf{K}^{+}(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)).

In the first section we set up preliminaries on liftings of modules, our approach to Problem 6. In the second section we consider the ordinary case, i.e., p∤|G|p\nmid|G|, in particular, we prove Theorem 8. The final section is devoted to the general case and contains a discussion of Conjecture 9.

1. Preliminaries

Let 𝕆\mathbb{O} be a discrete valuation ring, 𝕀=(ϖ)\mathbb{I}=(\varpi) – its maximal ideal with uniformiser ϖ\varpi. We also consider its residue field 𝔽≔𝕆/𝕀\mathbb{F}\coloneqq\mathbb{O}/\mathbb{I} and its fraction field 𝕂≔Q⁡(𝕆)\mathbb{K}\coloneqq Q(\mathbb{O}).

Let AA be an 𝕆\mathbb{O}-order, that is, an associative 𝕆\mathbb{O}-algebra, finitely generated projective as an 𝕆\mathbb{O}-module. Given a ring homomorphism ϕ:𝕆→R\phi:\mathbb{O}\rightarrow R, by AϕA_{\phi} or ARA_{R}, when ϕ\phi is clear by default, we denote the specialisation R⊗𝕆AR\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}A. The two key specialisations come from the two points of Spec​(𝕆)\mbox{Spec}(\mathbb{O}): the algebras A𝕂A_{\mathbb{K}} and A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}} are finite-dimensional of the same dimension.

Lemma 1.1.

The restriction to the Jacobson radicals ψ:J⁡(A)→J⁡(A𝔽)\psi:J(A)\rightarrow J(A_{\mathbb{F}}) of the natural homomorphism ψ:A→A𝔽\psi:A\rightarrow A_{\mathbb{F}} is surjective. Furthermore, J⁡(A)=ψ−1​(J⁡(A𝔽))J(A)=\psi^{-1}(J(A_{\mathbb{F}})).

Proof.

Since ψ\psi is surjective, ψ⁡(J⁡(A))⊆J⁡(A𝔽)\psi(J(A))\subseteq J(A_{\mathbb{F}}) and J⁡(A)⊆ψ−1​(J⁡(A𝔽))J(A)\subseteq\psi^{-1}(J(A_{\mathbb{F}})).

Now consider a simple AA-module MM. The multiplication by ϖ\varpi is a homomorphism M→MM\rightarrow M. By Schur’s Lemma, it is either zero or an automorphism. Note further that it cannot be an automorphism. Suppose it is. Then M=𝕂⊗𝕆MM=\mathbb{K}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}M is already an A𝕂A_{\mathbb{K}}-module. Choose finitely many generators a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n} of the 𝕆\mathbb{O}-module AA and a nonzero m∈Mm\in M. Let M′⊆MM^{\prime}\subseteq M be the 𝕆\mathbb{O}-submodule generated by a1​m,…,an​ma_{1}m,\ldots,a_{n}m. Clearly, M′M^{\prime} is an AA-submodule. By simplicity, M′=MM^{\prime}=M, which is impossible for a 𝕂\mathbb{K}-vector space.

Hence, ϖ​M=0\varpi M=0 and MM is an A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module. It follows that J⁡(A)J(A) and J⁡(A𝔽)J(A_{\mathbb{F}}) consist of the annihilators of the same set of modules. Consequently, ψ:J⁡(A)→J⁡(A𝔽)\psi:J(A)\rightarrow J(A_{\mathbb{F}}) is surjective and J⁡(A)=ψ−1​(J⁡(A𝔽))J(A)=\psi^{-1}(J(A_{\mathbb{F}})). ∎

Corollary 1.2.

The rings A/J⁡(A)A/J(A) and A𝔽/J⁡(A𝔽)A_{\mathbb{F}}/J(A_{\mathbb{F}}) are isomorphic.

We need to talk about lifting of modules. Let M𝔽M_{\mathbb{F}} be an A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module. We say that an AA-module MM is its lifting if MM is a projective 𝕆\mathbb{O}-module and M𝔽≅𝔽⊗𝕆MM_{\mathbb{F}}\cong\mathbb{F}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}M as A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-modules. The following observation is useful:

Lemma 1.3.

[5, Th. 30.11] Suppose MM is a lifting of M𝔽M_{\mathbb{F}}. The AA-module MM is projective if and only if the A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module M𝔽M_{\mathbb{F}} is projective.

We are ready for our main criterion, a handy supplement to Proposition 5.

Proposition 1.4.

The following conditions for the 𝕆\mathbb{O}-order AA are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    AA is semiperfect.

  2. (2)

    Every idempotent of A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}} can be lifted to an idempotent of AA.

  3. (3)

    Every principal indecomposable A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module admits a lifting.

  4. (4)

    Every finitely generated projective A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module admits a lifting.

Proof.

The equivalence (1)⇔(2)(1)\Leftrightarrow(2) follows from Corollary 1.2. Indeed, it ensures that A/J⁡(A)A/J(A) is a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra. By Proposition 5, AA is semiperfect if and only if all idempotents of A/J⁡(A)≅A𝔽/J⁡(A𝔽)A/J(A)\cong A_{\mathbb{F}}/J(A_{\mathbb{F}}) can be lifted to AA. It remains to compare idempotents in three algebras

A→𝜓A𝔽→𝜋A/J⁡(A)≅A𝔽/J⁡(A𝔽).A\xrightarrow{\psi}A_{\mathbb{F}}\xrightarrow{\pi}A/J(A)\cong A_{\mathbb{F}}/J(A_{\mathbb{F}})\,.

Indeed, an idempotent e∈A/J⁡(A)e\in A/J(A) can always be lifted to an idempotent e1∈A𝔽e_{1}\in A_{\mathbb{F}} because J⁡(A𝔽)J(A_{\mathbb{F}}) is nilpotent. Now use (2)(2) to lift it to an idempotent e2∈Ae_{2}\in A. This proves (1)(1).

In the opposite direction, assume (1)(1). Pick an idempotent e∈A𝔽e\in A_{\mathbb{F}}, lift π⁡(e)\pi(e) to an idempotent e1∈Ae_{1}\in A. This proves (2)(2).

The implication (1)⇒(4)(1)\Rightarrow(4) is contained within Proposition 5. Indeed, let P𝔽P_{\mathbb{F}} be a finitely generated projective A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module. As an AA-module, it is also finitely generated. Proposition 5 yields us an AA-projective cover π:P↠P𝔽\pi:P\twoheadrightarrow P_{\mathbb{F}}. Note that AA-projectivity implies 𝕆\mathbb{O}-projectivity.

Since ϖ​P𝔽=0\varpi P_{\mathbb{F}}=0, we conclude that ker⁡π⊇ϖ​P\ker\pi\supseteq\varpi P. The induced AA-module homomorphism π′\pi^{\prime} yields a decomposition

π:P→𝜓P/ϖ​P→π′P𝔽.\pi:P\xrightarrow{\psi}P/\varpi P\xrightarrow{\pi^{\prime}}P_{\mathbb{F}}\,.

Since P/ϖ​PP/\varpi P is an A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module, projectivity of P𝔽P_{\mathbb{F}} implies that π′\pi^{\prime} is split: P/ϖ​P=M⊕P𝔽P/\varpi P=M\oplus P_{\mathbb{F}} for another submodule MM. Hence,

P=ψ−1​(M)+ψ−1​(P𝔽)⊆ker⁡(π)+ψ−1​(P𝔽).P=\psi^{-1}(M)+\psi^{-1}(P_{\mathbb{F}})\subseteq\ker(\pi)+\psi^{-1}(P_{\mathbb{F}})\,.

Since ker⁡(π)\ker(\pi) is superfluous, P=ψ−1​(P𝔽)P=\psi^{-1}(P_{\mathbb{F}}) and M=0M=0. Therefore, ker⁡π=ϖ​P\ker\pi=\varpi P and P⊗𝕆𝔽≅P𝔽P\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{F}\cong P_{\mathbb{F}}, so that PP is a lifting.

To prove (3)⇒(1)(3)\Rightarrow(1), we construct a projective cover of a simple AA-module MM. By Corollary 1.2, MM is an A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module. Let P𝔽​(M)P_{\mathbb{F}}(M) be its A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-projective cover. Since P𝔽​(M)P_{\mathbb{F}}(M) is a principal indecomposable, it admits a lifting PP. We claim that PP is an AA-projective cover of MM. Indeed, it is projective by Lemma 1.3 and we have surjective homomorphisms of A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}} modules

π:P→𝜓P𝔽​(M)→π′M.\pi:P\xrightarrow{\psi}P_{\mathbb{F}}(M)\xrightarrow{\pi^{\prime}}M\,.

It remains to argue that ker⁡(π)\ker(\pi) is superfluous. Assume L+ker⁡(π)=PL+\ker(\pi)=P. It follows that ψ⁡(L)+ker⁡(π′)=P𝔽​(M)\psi(L)+\ker(\pi^{\prime})=P_{\mathbb{F}}(M). Since π′\pi^{\prime} is an A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-projective cover, ker⁡(π′)\ker(\pi^{\prime}) is superfluous and ψ​(L)=P𝔽​(M)\psi(L)=P_{\mathbb{F}}(M). It follows that L+ker⁡(ψ)=L+ϖ​P=PL+\ker(\psi)=L+\varpi P=P. Observe that ψ\psi is an 𝕆\mathbb{O}-module projective cover. Hence, ker⁡(ψ)\ker(\psi) is 𝕆\mathbb{O}-superfluous and L=PL=P.

The final implication (4)⇒(3)(4)\Rightarrow(3) is obvious. ∎

The final well-known corollary is immediate since completeness of 𝕆\mathbb{O} enables lifting of idempotents.

Corollary 1.5.

If 𝕆\mathbb{O} is complete, AA is semiperfect.

2. The semisimple case

Before specialising to the case of the group algebra, we make several general observations in the case, when A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}} is semisimple. The following observation is not fully routine because semisimplicity (in contrast to separability) is not an open condition:

Lemma 2.1.

If A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}} is semisimple, then A𝕂A_{\mathbb{K}} is semisimple.

Proof.

Suppose A𝕂A_{\mathbb{K}} is not semisimple. Then I≔A∩J⁡(A𝕂)I\coloneqq A\cap J(A_{\mathbb{K}}) is a non-zero nilpotent ideal of AA. Since A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}} is semisimple, it has no nilpotent ideals. Therefore, ψ⁡(I)=0\psi(I)=0 and I⊆ϖ​A=ker⁡ψI\subseteq\varpi A=\ker\psi, where ψ:A→A𝔽\psi:A\rightarrow A_{\mathbb{F}} is the reduction homomorphism.

Consider now I′=ϖ−1​I≔{x∈A∣ϖ​x∈I}I^{\prime}=\varpi^{-1}I\coloneqq\{x\in A\,\mid\,\varpi x\in I\}. Clearly, I′I^{\prime} is still a subset of J⁡(A𝕂)J(A_{\mathbb{K}}). Hence, I′=II^{\prime}=I. Now pick a nonzero element ϖn​a∈I\varpi^{n}a\in I with a∈A∖ϖ​Aa\in A\setminus\varpi A and the smallest possible nn. Since I⊆ϖ​AI\subseteq\varpi A, n≥1n\geq 1. Then ϖn−1​a∈I′\varpi^{n-1}a\in I^{\prime}, proving that I′≠II^{\prime}\neq I, a contradiction. ∎

In light of Lemma 2.1, the next step is to compare Artin-Wedderburn decompositions. Let us fix them:

(4) A𝔽≅Mn1​(F1)⊕…⊕Mnk​(Fk),A𝕂≅Mm1​(K1)⊕…⊕Mmt​(Kt)A_{\mathbb{F}}\cong M_{n_{1}}(F_{1})\oplus\ldots\oplus M_{n_{k}}(F_{k}),\quad A_{\mathbb{K}}\cong M_{m_{1}}(K_{1})\oplus\ldots\oplus M_{m_{t}}(K_{t})

where FiF_{i}, KiK_{i} are finite-dimensional division algebras over 𝔽\mathbb{F} and 𝕂\mathbb{K}, respectively. By ι⁡(Fi)≔dimZ⁡(Fi)Fi\iota(F_{i})\coloneqq\sqrt{\dim_{Z(F_{i})}F_{i}}, ι⁡(Ki)≔dimZ⁡(Ki)Ki\iota(K_{i})\coloneqq\sqrt{\dim_{Z(K_{i})}K_{i}} we denote their Schur indices.

Proposition 2.2.

Suppose that A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}} is semisimple with Artin-Wedderburn decompositions as in (4). In addition to Proposition 1.4, the following conditions for the 𝕆\mathbb{O}-order AA are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    AA is semiperfect.

  2. (2)

    Every simple A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module admits a lifting.

Let us assume further that AA is a maximal order. Then the above conditions are also equivalent to the following two conditions.

  1. (3)

    The numbers of simple modules are equal: k=tk=t. Furthermore, after a suitable permutation every simple A𝕂A_{\mathbb{K}}-module KimiK_{i}^{m_{i}} admits an AA-lattice MiM_{i} such that the A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-modules Mi⊗𝕆𝔽M_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{F} and FiniF_{i}^{n_{i}} are isomorphic.

  2. (4)

    The numbers of simple modules are equal: k=tk=t. Furthermore, after a suitable permutation for every ii we have ni=min_{i}=m_{i}, ι⁡(Fi)=ι⁡(Ki)\iota(F_{i})=\iota(K_{i}) and every division algebra KiK_{i} admits an 𝕆\mathbb{O}-order LiL_{i} such that the 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras Li⊗𝕆𝔽L_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{F} and FiF_{i} are isomorphic.

Proof.

The implication (3)⇒(2)(3)\Rightarrow(2) is obvious: the AA-module MiM_{i} is an explicit lifting of a simple A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module FiniF_{i}^{n_{i}}.

The equivalence (2)⇔(1)(2)\Leftrightarrow(1) follows from Proposition 1.4. Since A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}} is semisimple, its principal indecomposable modules are the same as simple modules. By Proposition 1.4, they admit liftings.

To prove the implication (3)⇒(4)(3)\Rightarrow(4), note that MiM_{i} is a projective AA-module by Lemma 1.3. Define LiL_{i} as the endomorphism ring Li≔EndA​MiL_{i}\coloneqq\mbox{End}_{A}M_{i}. Since MiM_{i} is AA-projective, the natural map

Li→EndA𝔽​Fini≅FiL_{i}\rightarrow\mbox{End}_{A_{\mathbb{F}}}F_{i}^{n_{i}}\cong F_{i}

is surjective and Li⊗𝕆𝔽≅FiL_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{F}\cong F_{i}. Observe that the second natural map

ϕ:Li→Li⊗𝕆𝕂→EndA𝕂​(Mi⊗𝕆𝕂)≅EndA𝕂​Kimi≅Ki\phi:L_{i}\rightarrow L_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{K}\rightarrow\mbox{End}_{A_{\mathbb{K}}}(M_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{K})\cong\mbox{End}_{A_{\mathbb{K}}}K_{i}^{m_{i}}\cong K_{i}

is injective. If w∈Liw\in L_{i} and w≠0w\neq 0, then w⁡(x)≠0w(x)\neq 0 for some x∈Mi⊆Kimix\in M_{i}\subseteq K_{i}^{m_{i}}. Hence, ϕ​(w)​(x)≠0\phi(w)(x)\neq 0 and ϕ⁡(w)≠0\phi(w)\neq 0.

Now observe that ϕ⁡(Li)≅Li\phi(L_{i})\cong L_{i} is a lattice in KiK_{i}. Pick any w∈Kiw\in K_{i}. For some natural nn we have ϖn​w​(Mi)⊆Mi\varpi^{n}w(M_{i})\subseteq M_{i}. Thus, ϖn​w∈ϕ⁡(Li)\varpi^{n}w\in\phi(L_{i}).

The outstanding requirements follow immediately: ni=min_{i}=m_{i} and ι⁡(Ki)=ι⁡(Fi)\iota(K_{i})=\iota(F_{i}) .

The remaining implications utilise the requirement that AA is a maximal order.

Let us prove (1)⇒(3)(1)\Rightarrow(3). Note that a simple A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-module FiniF_{i}^{n_{i}} has a form A𝔽​eA_{\mathbb{F}}e for a minimal idempotent ee in A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}. It can be lifted to a minimal idempotent e~∈A\tilde{e}\in A. Observe that Mi≔A​e~M_{i}\coloneqq A\tilde{e} is a lifting of FiniF_{i}^{n_{i}}. Since e~\tilde{e} is minimal, MiM_{i} is an indecomposable AA-module. By [5, Th. 26.12], A𝕂​e~A_{\mathbb{K}}\tilde{e} is a simple A𝕂A_{\mathbb{K}}-module. After a suitable permutation, it is KimiK_{i}^{m_{i}}. The implication is proved.

The final implication (4)⇒(2)(4)\Rightarrow(2) is an immediate corollary of the structure theorem for maximal orders. By [5, Th. 26.20], A=A1⊕…⊕AtA=A_{1}\oplus\ldots\oplus A_{t} where each AiA_{i} is a maximal order in Mmi​(Ki)M_{m_{i}}(K_{i}). By [5, Th. 26.23], after a change of basis, we have Ai=Mmi​(Bi)A_{i}=M_{m_{i}}(B_{i}) for a maximal order Bi≤KiB_{i}\leq K_{i}, and moreover, Bi⊇LiB_{i}\supseteq L_{i}. It follows that the natural map

Fi≅Li⊗𝕆𝔽→Bi⊗𝕆𝔽F_{i}\cong L_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{F}\rightarrow B_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{F}

is an isomorphism. Hence, Ai⊗𝕆𝔽≅Mni​(Fi)A_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{O}}\mathbb{F}\cong M_{n_{i}}(F_{i}) and all simple A𝔽A_{\mathbb{F}}-modules have liftings. ∎

Let us now specialise to the situation of our primary concern: A≔𝕆​GA\coloneqq\mathbb{O}G for a finite group GG, where 𝕆≔ℤ(p)\mathbb{O}\coloneqq\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}, the localisation of the integers at the prime pp, p∤|G|p\nmid|G|. Note that 𝔽=ℤ(p)/p​ℤ(p)≅𝔽p\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}/p\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}\cong\mathbb{F}_{p} and 𝕂=ℚ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{Q}, the rational numbers. Observe that AA is a maximal order in ℚ​G\mathbb{Q}G [5, Prop. 27.1] so that Proposition 2.2 is fully applicable. Let us use it to examine two examples.

Example 2.3.

Let G=CnG=C_{n}, p∤np\nmid n, a slight generalisation of (2). The following argument is essentially a proof of the last two statements of Proposition 7. Clearly,

ℚ​G≅⨁d|nℚ⁡(1d)≅⨁d|nℚ⁡[z](Ψd​(z)),𝔽p​G≅⨁i𝔽p​[z](ψi​(z))\mathbb{Q}G\cong\bigoplus_{d|n}\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[d]{1})\cong\bigoplus_{d|n}\dfrac{\mathbb{Q}[z]}{(\Psi_{d}(z))},\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}G\cong\bigoplus_{i}\dfrac{\mathbb{F}_{p}[z]}{(\psi_{i}(z))}

where Ψd\Psi_{d} is the dd-th cyclotomic polynomial and ψi\psi_{i} are “cyclotomic polynomials” modulo pp, i.e., prime factors of zn−1∈𝔽p​[z]z^{n}-1\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[z]. All Schur indices are equal to 1. By Proposition 2.2 and [12, Th 3.5], the following three conditions are equivalent:

  • •

    ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect,

  • •

    for each d|nd\mid n the polynomial Ψd​(z)\Psi_{d}(z) remains irreducible modulo pp,

  • •

    for each d|nd\mid n the order of pp in the group GL1​(ℤ/(d))\mbox{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{Z}/(d)) is φ⁡(d)\varphi(d) (maximal allowed by Euler’s Theorem).

Let us now see an example where the Schur index plays a role.

Example 2.4.

Let G=Q8G=Q_{8}, the quaternion group of order 88, p≠2p\neq 2. Then

ℚ​G≅ℚ⊕4⊕ℍℚ,𝔽p​G≅𝔽p⊕4⊕M2​(𝔽p)\mathbb{Q}G\cong\mathbb{Q}^{\oplus 4}\oplus\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{Q}},\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}G\cong{\mathbb{F}}_{p}^{\oplus 4}\oplus M_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p})

where ℍℚ{\mathbb{H}}_{\mathbb{Q}} is the quaternion algebra over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. Then ι⁡(ℍℚ)=2≠1=ι⁡(𝔽p)\iota(\mathbb{H}_{\mathbb{Q}})=2\neq 1=\iota(\mathbb{F}_{p}). By Proposition 2.2, ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is not semiperfect.

Let us recall the well-known facts about the Artin-Wedderburn decomposition of ℚ​G\mathbb{Q}G in terms of its complex characters. They are a combination of the Brauer-Fein theorem [7] and various standard facts [13, Section 12.2].

Lemma 2.5.

Let GG be a finite group with the Artin-Wedderburn decomposition of A𝕂=ℚ​GA_{\mathbb{K}}=\mathbb{Q}G as in (4). Let Zi≔Z⁡(Ki)Z_{i}\coloneqq Z(K_{i}), si=dimℚZis_{i}=\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}Z_{i} and di=ι⁡(Ki)d_{i}=\iota(K_{i}). The following statements hold.

  1. i)

    For each summand Mmi​(Ki)M_{m_{i}}(K_{i}), we have Mmi​(Ki)⊗ℚℚ¯≅Mmi​di​(ℚ¯)⊕siM_{m_{i}}(K_{i})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\bar{\mathbb{Q}}\cong M_{m_{i}d_{i}}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})^{\oplus s_{i}}, which yields sis_{i} distinct complex characters χi,1,…,χi,si\chi_{i,1},\ldots,\chi_{i,s_{i}} of degree mi​dim_{i}d_{i}.

  2. ii)

    The set of complex irreducible characters is a disjoint union

    Irr⁡(G)=∐i=1t{χi,1,…,χi,si}.\Irr(G)\;=\;\coprod_{i=1}^{t}\{\chi_{i,1},\ldots,\chi_{i,s_{i}}\}\,.
  3. iii)

    For each ii and j∈{1,…,si}j\in\{1,\ldots,s_{i}\} the field ZiZ_{i} is ℚ⁡(χi,j)\mathbb{Q}(\chi_{i,j}), the field of values of the character.

  4. iv)

    For each ii, the extension Zi⊇ℚZ_{i}\supseteq\mathbb{Q} is Galois.

  5. v)

    The characters χi,1,…,χi,si\chi_{i,1},\ldots,\chi_{i,s_{i}} constitute one Gal​(Zi/ℚ)\textup{Gal}(Z_{i}/\mathbb{Q})-orbit.

Now, we are ready to prove the main theorem.

Proof.

(of Theorem 8) Recall that for an algebraic number field 𝕂\mathbb{K}, the ring 𝒪𝕂/(p)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{K}}/(p) of integers modulo pp can be either a field, or a direct sum of at least two fields, or a non-reduced ring. These mutually exclusive possibilities mean that the prime pp is correspondingly either inert in 𝕂\mathbb{K}, or split in 𝕂\mathbb{K}, or ramified in 𝕂\mathbb{K}.

Now A=ℤ(p)​GA={{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G has Artin-Wedderburn decompositions (4). Since AA is a maximal order (cf. the proof of (4)⇒(2)(4)\Rightarrow(2) of Proposition 2.2), we can write

(5) ℤ(p)G≅Mm1(B1)⊕…⊕Mmt(Bt),𝔽pG≅⊕i=1tMmi(Bi⊗ℤ(p)𝔽p){{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G\cong M_{m_{1}}(B_{1})\oplus\ldots\oplus M_{m_{t}}(B_{t})\,,\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}G\cong\oplus_{i=1}^{t}M_{m_{i}}(B_{i}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}\mathbb{F}_{p})

where BiB_{i} is a maximal order in KiK_{i}.

By Proposition 2.2, AA is semiperfect if and only Bi⊗ℤ(p)𝔽≅FiB_{i}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}\mathbb{F}\cong F_{i} for all ii, after a suitable permutation of indices.

We proceed to prove the “only if” direction. By the Little Wedderburn Theorem, all FiF_{i} are finite fields. This forces commutativity of both BiB_{i} and KiK_{i}. Since Ki=ℚ⁡(χi,j)K_{i}=\mathbb{Q}(\chi_{i,j}) is commutative for all ii and jj, we conclude that ι⁡(χ)=1\iota(\chi)=1 for all χ∈Irr⁡(G)\chi\in\Irr(G). Further, we can rewrite the decompositions (5) as

(6) ℤ(p)G≅⊕i=1tMmi(𝒪ℚ⁡(χi,1)),𝔽pG≅⊕i=1tMmi(𝒪ℚ⁡(χi,1)/(p)),{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G\cong\oplus_{i=1}^{t}M_{m_{i}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\chi_{i,1})})\,,\quad\mathbb{F}_{p}G\cong\oplus_{i=1}^{t}M_{m_{i}}(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\chi_{i,1})}/(p)\,)\,,

where Proposition 2.2 forces all 𝒪ℚ⁡(χ)⊗ℤ(p)𝔽p\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\chi)}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}\mathbb{F}_{p} to be fields. This means that the prime pp is inert in all ℚ⁡(χ)\mathbb{Q}(\chi).

For the “if” direction, observe that the first condition (all ι⁡(χ)=1\iota(\chi)=1) enables us to write the Artin-Wedderburn decompositions as in (6). Now the second condition ensures that all 𝒪ℚ⁡(χ)⊗ℤ(p)𝔽p\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\chi)}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}\mathbb{F}_{p} are fields. By Proposition 2.2, ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect. ∎

3. The general case

Let us consider the general case now. Note that if p∤|G|p\nmid|G|, ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is not a maximal order [5, Prop. 27.1]. This creates additional challenges. However, many standard results still hold under the assumption that ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect [5, Ch. 17]. In particular, we can settle the only-if direction of Conjecture 9.

Proposition 3.1.

If the ring ℤ(p)​G\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G is semiperfect, then α⁡(𝐆+​(ℚ​G))⊇β⁡(𝐊+​(𝔽p​G))\alpha(\mathbf{G}^{+}(\mathbb{Q}G))\supseteq\beta(\mathbf{K}^{+}(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)).

Proof.

The reduction modulo pp yields an isomorphism 𝐊+​(ℤ(p)​G)→≅𝐊+​(𝔽p​G)\mathbf{K}^{+}({{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G)\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbf{K}^{+}(\mathbb{F}_{p}G), cf. [5, Th. 18.2]. From the commutativity of the Cartan-Brauer Triangle [5, Prop. 18.5], it suffices to observe that the natural map

γ:𝐊⁡(ℤ(p)​G)→𝐆⁡(ℚ​G),[M]↦[ℚ⊗ℤ(p)M]\gamma:\mathbf{K}({{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G)\rightarrow\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{Q}G),\quad[M]\mapsto[\mathbb{Q}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}M]

takes 𝐊+​(ℤ(p)​G)\mathbf{K}^{+}({{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G) to 𝐆+​(ℚ​G)\mathbf{G}^{+}(\mathbb{Q}G). But this is obvious because ℚ⊗ℤ(p)M\mathbb{Q}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}M can be wrtten as a finite direct sum of simple ℚ​G\mathbb{Q}G-modules. ∎

Our second observation is that Conjecture 9 holds true under a condition on the Sylow pp-subgroup. Note that this trivially covers the case p∤|G|p\nmid|G|. Furthermore, Conjecture 9 reduces to Theorem 8 in this case, and therefore, holds.

Proposition 3.2.

Suppose the group GG is a semidirect product P⋊HP\rtimes H of its Sylow pp-subgroup PP and a p′p^{\prime}-subgroup HH. The following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    α⁡(𝐆+​(ℚ​G))⊇β⁡(𝐊+​(𝔽p​G))\alpha(\mathbf{G}^{+}(\mathbb{Q}G))\supseteq\beta(\mathbf{K}^{+}(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)).

  2. (2)

    ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect.

  3. (3)

    ℤ(p)​H{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}H is semiperfect.

Proof.

Proposition 3.1 asserts (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1).

The implication (3)⇒(2)(3)\Rightarrow(2) is part (3) of Proposition 7.

Let us prove the final implication (1)⇒(3)(1)\Rightarrow(3). By IRI_{R} we denote the ideal (1−x)x∈P(1-x)_{x\in P} in the group algebra R​GRG. Since PP is normal,

IR=ker⁡(R​G→R​H),R​G/IR≅R​H​ and ​I𝔽p=J⁡(𝔽p​G).I_{R}=\ker(RG\rightarrow RH),\ \ RG/I_{R}\cong RH\ \mbox{ and }\ I_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}=J(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)\,.\

Observe that for every ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G-module MM, we have isomorphisms of 𝔽p​H\mathbb{F}_{p}H-modules

𝔽p​H⊗𝔽p​G(𝔽p⊗ℤ(p)M)≅𝔽p⊗ℤ(p)(ℤ(p)​H⊗ℤ(p)​GM)≅𝔽p​H⊗ℤ(p)​GM,\mathbb{F}_{p}H\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{p}G}(\mathbb{F}_{p}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}M)\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}({\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}H\otimes_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G}M)\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}H\otimes_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G}M,

which, in its turn, allows us to conclude that the diagram

𝐆+​(ℚ​G)→αG𝐆+​(𝔽p​G)M↦ℚ​H⊗ℚ​GM≅M/(Iℚ​M)↓γℚγ𝔽p↓𝐆+​(ℚ​H)→αH𝐆+​(𝔽p​H)\begin{CD}\mathbf{G}^{+}(\mathbb{Q}G)@>{}>{\alpha_{G}}>\mathbf{G}^{+}(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)\\ @V{M\mapsto\mathbb{Q}H\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}G}M\cong M/(I_{\mathbb{Q}}M)}V{\gamma_{\mathbb{Q}}}V@V{\gamma_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}}V{}V\\ \mathbf{G}^{+}(\mathbb{Q}H)@>{\alpha_{H}}>{}>\mathbf{G}^{+}(\mathbb{F}_{p}H)\end{CD}

is commutative. Let us fix the Artin-Wedderburn decompositions for HH as in (4), so that we have the sets of simple modules

Irr⁡(𝔽p​G)=Irr⁡(𝔽p​H)={Fini}i=1,…,k,Irr⁡(ℚ​H)={Kimi}i=1,…,t⊆Irr⁡(ℚ​G),\Irr(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)=\Irr(\mathbb{F}_{p}H)=\{F^{n_{i}}_{i}\}_{i=1,\ldots,k},\ \Irr(\mathbb{Q}H)=\{K_{i}^{m_{i}}\}_{i=1,\ldots,t}\subseteq\Irr(\mathbb{Q}G),

whose classes constitute ℤ\mathbb{Z}-bases of the four Grothendieck groups in the diagram. Let PiP_{i} be the 𝔽p​G\mathbb{F}_{p}G-projective cover of FiniF_{i}^{n_{i}}. Notice that

γ𝔽p​([Pi])=γ𝔽p​([Fini])=[Fini].\gamma_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}([P_{i}])=\gamma_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}([F_{i}^{n_{i}}])=[F_{i}^{n_{i}}]\,.

Condition (1) tells us that the classes [Pi][P_{i}] belong to the image of αG\alpha_{G}. Hence, the composition γ𝔽p∘αG=αH∘γℚ\gamma_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}\circ\alpha_{G}=\alpha_{H}\circ\gamma_{\mathbb{Q}} is surjective. Now observe that

L∈Irr⁡(ℚ​G)⟹γℚ​([L])={[L] if ​L∈Irr⁡(ℚ​H),0 if ​L∉Irr⁡(ℚ​H).L\in\Irr(\mathbb{Q}G)\ \Longrightarrow\ \gamma_{\mathbb{Q}}([L])=\begin{cases}[L]&\mbox{ if }L\in\Irr(\mathbb{Q}H),\\ 0&\mbox{ if }L\not\in\Irr(\mathbb{Q}H).\end{cases}

Hence, γℚ\gamma_{\mathbb{Q}} is surjective, and therefore, αH\alpha_{H} is surjective. Let LiL_{i} be a maximal order in KiK_{i}, si=ι⁡(Ki)s_{i}=\iota(K_{i}). Semisimplicity of 𝔽p​H\mathbb{F}_{p}H means that pp cannot be ramified in the field Z⁡(Ki)Z(K_{i}). Computationally,

αH​([Kimi])=[(Li⊗ℤ(p)𝔽p)mi]=si​∑j∈X⁡(i)[Fjnj]\alpha_{H}([K_{i}^{m_{i}}])=[(L_{i}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}\mathbb{F}_{p})^{m_{i}}]=s_{i}\sum_{j\in X(i)}[F_{j}^{n_{j}}]

where the sets of indices X⁡(i)X(i) do not intersect for different ii. Because of that, surjectivity of αH\alpha_{H} implies that si=1s_{i}=1 and each set of indices X⁡(i)X(i) consist of a single index. Hence, the conditions of Theorem 8 are met for HH and ℤ(p)​H{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}H is semiperfect.

∎

The second condition of Conjecture 9 essentially means that every projective 𝔽p​G\mathbb{F}_{p}G-module PP can be written in the KK-theory as

[P]=∑V∈Irr⁡(ℚ​G)NV​[𝔽p⊗ℤ(p)V~]∈𝐆⁡(𝔽p​G) with ​NV∈ℕ[P]=\sum_{V\in\Irr(\mathbb{Q}G)}N_{V}[\mathbb{F}_{p}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}\widetilde{V}]\in\mathbf{G}(\mathbb{F}_{p}G)\quad\mbox{ with }N_{V}\in\mathbb{N}

where V~\widetilde{V} are ℤ(p)​G{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G}-lattices in the ℚ​G\mathbb{Q}G-modules VV. This condition can be strengthened. We say that a filtration on an 𝔽p​G\mathbb{F}_{p}G-module MM

M=Mk≥Mk−1≥…≥M1≥M0=0M=M_{k}\geq M_{k-1}\geq\ldots\geq M_{1}\geq M_{0}=0

is a Brauer-Humphreys filtration if each consequent quotient Mi/Mi−1M_{i}/M_{i-1} is isomorphic to 𝔽p⊗ℤ(p)V~\mathbb{F}_{p}\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}\widetilde{V} where V~\widetilde{V} is a ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G-lattice in a simple ℚ​G\mathbb{Q}G-module VV.

Proposition 3.3.

If every projective indecomposable 𝔽p​G\mathbb{F}_{p}G-module has a Brauer-Humphreys filtration, then ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect.

Proof.

Let PP be a projective indecomposable 𝔽p​G\mathbb{F}_{p}G-module, PiP_{i} – its Brauer-Humphreys filtration. We construct the lifting P~i\widetilde{P}_{i} of each PiP_{i} recursively, i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\ldots,n.

The definition of the filtration yields P~1\widetilde{P}_{1}.

Now suppose P~i\widetilde{P}_{i} is constructed. Let V~\widetilde{V} be a lifting of Pi+1/PiP_{i+1}/P_{i}. By [5, Cor. 25.6], the natural map

ψ=``𝔽p⊗ℤ−":Extℤ(p)​G1(Pi~,V~)→≅Ext𝔽p​G1(Pi,V)\psi=``\mathbb{F}_{p}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\,-\,":\mbox{Ext}^{1}_{{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G}(\widetilde{P_{i}},\widetilde{V})\xrightarrow{\cong}\mbox{Ext}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}G}({P_{i}},{V})

is an isomorphism. A ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G-module representing ψ−1​(Pi+1)\psi^{-1}(P_{i+1}) is a lifting of Pi+1P_{i+1}.

By Proposition 1.4, ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G is semiperfect. ∎

We finish the paper with an investigation of the semiperfectness of ℤ(p)​G{{\mathbb{Z}}_{(p)}}G for the smallest simple non-abelian group.
